title: Senators demand crackdown on wildfire "prediction markets"
gist: US senators from five states have formally asked the CFTC to crack down on prediction markets listing contracts on wildfires, citing arson and insider-trading risk; Kalshi has voluntarily banned such markets while Polymarket defends them as information infrastructure and says it currently lists none.

themes.theme: CFTC regulatory pressure on event contracts

insights.claim: A group of US senators representing Oregon, California, Nevada, Minnesota and New Hampshire sent a public letter on Monday asking the CFTC about its plans to crack down on prediction markets offering contracts on wildfires.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Congressional letters to the CFTC are the standard leading indicator of rulemaking or enforcement against event-contract categories; watch for a follow-on CFTC action that could set precedent for disaster and catastrophe contracts broadly.
insights.quote: Offering bets on destructive wildfires threatens to minimize communities’ suffering, all so the rich and powerful can profit

insights.claim: The senators' letter singles out Polymarket for hosting bets in January 2025 on the Los Angeles wildfires, naming a specific platform rather than the category in the abstract.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Named-entity targeting in a Congressional letter raises the odds that any CFTC action lands asymmetrically on one venue rather than industry-wide, which matters for relative platform risk.

insights.claim: The CFTC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the senators' letter, leaving the agency's posture on disaster-linked contracts unstated.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Regulatory silence keeps the tail risk live; the absence of a quick dismissal is itself mildly negative for platforms listing catastrophe contracts.
insights.locator: The CFTC did not immediately respond

insights.claim: The senators argue that wildfire contracts create a physical-world manipulation channel: bettors could be tempted to commit arson, or to influence fires already burning, to settle their positions in the money.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: This is the strongest regulatory argument against real-world-outcome contracts and generalizes to any market whose settlement a small actor can physically influence — a structural ceiling on what event-contract venues can list.
insights.quote: By offering contracts on fires, prediction market sites run the risk of encouraging people to influence fires that have already started, creating additional concerns around public safety and insider trading.

insights.claim: State and local fire officials, not just legislators, are the cited source for the arson-incentive concern, giving the regulatory argument operational rather than purely political backing.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Operational-agency support makes the claim harder for platforms to dismiss as grandstanding and increases the chance it survives into formal rulemaking language.
insights.locator: There’s also the heightened risk—according to state and local fire officials

insights.claim: A UC Berkeley Fire Research Lab professor frames disaster prediction markets as a misallocation of societal energy, arguing resources should go to pre-event mitigation investment rather than monetizing outcomes.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The 'mitigate before, don't monetize after' frame is the intellectual counterweight to the information-discovery defense and will shape how catastrophe-contract policy is argued.
insights.quote: We should not focus our energy on monetizing the outcome of devastating natural disasters. Instead, we should focus our efforts on mitigating these events with targeting investments before they start

insights.claim: The president of Grassroots Wildland Firefighters, a nonprofit of current and former federal wildland firefighters, says her community is 'pretty disgusted' by wildfire betting markets, indicating organized frontline-responder opposition.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Sympathetic frontline constituencies are exactly the witnesses that turn a letter into a hearing; reputational risk for platforms compounds faster than legal risk here.
insights.quote: To think there are people hoping to make money off tragedy is beyond comprehension
insights.locator: Riva Duncan, the president of Grassroots Wildland Firefighters

themes.theme: Kalshi vs Polymarket divergence on listing policy

insights.claim: Kalshi has an explicit policy against listing wildfire markets, with a spokesperson stating the company bars them because such contracts 'create perverse incentives.'
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Voluntary self-restriction by the CFTC-regulated venue is a cheap regulatory hedge; it positions Kalshi as the compliant incumbent if rulemaking follows.
insights.locator: Kalshi is one of the major prediction markets

insights.claim: The two largest prediction markets have taken opposite policy stances on disaster contracts, so the sector no longer has a unified line to defend in front of regulators.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A split industry is easier to regulate piecemeal; expect the compliant venue to quietly benefit from rules written against the non-compliant one.
insights.quote: But its primary rival, Polymarket, has taken a different approach.

insights.claim: Polymarket's public defense is that it does not 'profit from outcomes' and that users come to the platform for information, framing the venue as an information utility rather than a gambling operator.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: The information-utility framing is the whole legal and PR strategy for event contracts; if regulators reject it for disasters, the same rejection threatens other socially sensitive categories.
insights.locator: A spokesperson for Polymarket told Ars

insights.claim: Polymarket argues that delisting disaster markets destroys information rather than preventing harm, claiming removal 'makes the most accurate information less accessible to the people who need it most.'
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: This is the strongest pro-listing argument and the one to test empirically; its credibility determines whether catastrophe contracts survive as a product category.
insights.quote: While we are not blind to the risks, removing these markets does not prevent a tragedy but makes the most accurate information less accessible to the people who need it most
insights.locator: While we are not blind to the risks

insights.claim: Polymarket's spokesperson declined to answer whether the platform claims by definition to provide the most accurate information to people experiencing a wildfire, and tried to place its statement that it currently lists no wildfire markets 'on background' after the fact.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Communications fragility around the core defense suggests the argument is not battle-tested; a company confident in the information thesis would defend it on the record.
insights.quote: Polymarket does not currently have any markets on wildfires and has not for some time.
insights.locator: In the same email, the spokesperson also noted

insights.claim: The letter landed while active wildfires burn across significant parts of the Pacific Northwest, with roughly a quarter of Spokane, Washington's population under evacuation orders and several hundred buildings already destroyed.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: Policy on catastrophe contracts is being written during a live catastrophe, which historically produces faster and blunter rules than off-cycle deliberation.
insights.locator: The public letter, which was issued Monday

insights.claim: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office announced the arrest of an arson suspect believed to have started one of the blazes threatening Spokane, giving the abstract arson-incentive argument a concrete contemporaneous case.
insights.speaker: Ars Contributors
insights.so_what: A real arson arrest in the same news cycle converts a speculative regulatory objection into a narrative regulators can point to, sharply raising the odds of action.
